Every claim in documentation—config options, file paths, command examples, setting names, and lists of events or fields—must be verified against actual source code or a live test run before publishing, rather than inferred from context or carried over from prior docs. For example, CLI examples like `cline connect telegram --restart -k <BOT-TOKEN>` must actually be executed, since argument-forwarding and flag-ordering bugs are easy to introduce and easy to miss otherwise; log file locations and setting keys (e.g., which process writes `cline-core-service.log`, or whether `cline.rollout.bundleOverride` differs for nightly builds) must be confirmed via source inspection or tools like `lsof`, not assumption.

If a documented feature, option, or environment variable is broken or non-functional (e.g., `CLINE_HOOKS_DIR` having no effect), remove it from the docs instead of describing it as "accepted but ignored" or silently broken — documenting a non-functional option invites misuse and implies it will be fixed soon. Only keep a "currently broken" caveat when a fix is concretely planned and the feature is central enough that removing it would be more disruptive than the caveat. Similarly, once a feature is fully deprecated (e.g., `.clineignore`), remove its documentation entirely rather than leaving it in an ambiguous "will be deprecated soon" state.

When documenting reference lists (event types, JSON output fields, supported tools), either make the list genuinely complete and verified, or explicitly state that it is non-exhaustive and tell readers how to handle unlisted or unrecognized items (e.g., "skip types you don't use") rather than implying full coverage.
